text.en: A seller brings guavas to the market and a buyer offers a very low price. The seller refuses, saying he would make a loss. Another buyer offers a fair price and the deal is done. A market is not only a place, it is a meeting of buyers and sellers who agree on a price. In this chapter we see how markets work, who takes part in them and how the government and consumers keep them fair.

Goods and services reach people, households and businesses through markets. Every market has a buyer and a seller. A buyer has a want, something they need or desire, and is willing and able to pay. A market helps people get things they cannot produce themselves. The famous economist Adam Smith said that prosperity comes from markets that develop when people need goods and services that they cannot create themselves.
The price is the amount of money a buyer pays for a good or service. Prices are generally determined by the interaction of demand from buyers and supply by sellers. Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at a particular price at a given time. Supply is the quantity that sellers are ready to offer. If many buyers want a thing and supply is small, the price rises. If supply is large and few want it, the price falls. If the seller fixes the price very low, he makes a loss and may stop selling. If the price is too high, buyers will not buy. In a fair market both sides agree on a price. If onion growers do not bring enough onions to the market, the price rises. Sometimes governments cap prices, but they must do so carefully to avoid shortages.
A physical market is where buyers can meet sellers in person, for vegetables, clothes, phones, medicines and more. Some services, like a haircut, need physical presence. An online market lets people transact from convenient places even thousands of kilometres apart, and manufacturers can buy components online to use as inputs in production. Trade across the borders of countries is also possible. Markets also have a history and place. A city's location on the west coast, for example, led to ports and road networks that continue to be important today. In Imphal, Manipur, the Ima Keithel market is run by women and sells vegetables, hand-loom cloth including traditional Manipuri attire, handicrafts, local produce and daily essentials.
A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from the producer or manufacturer and stores them in large warehouses. There are wholesale markets for grains and for chemicals, electronics, construction materials and automotive parts. Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell to consumers in small quantities. Distributors and aggregators bridge the gap when wholesalers find it difficult to reach many retailers because of distance and terrain, and they assess how much product retailers need. Markets also show producers what consumers would buy, so they guide production.
Markets work best when they are fair. The government monitors the interaction between consumers and producers and ensures fair prices, correct weights and good quality. It sets procedures for approving medicines and tests samples to check they meet standards. It restricts goods like single-use plastics that pollute and harm health. An ancient text, the Arthashastra, said that buyers should be given one-fiftieth part more as manasrava to make up for the ghee that sticks to the measuring can, showing that fair measures mattered long ago. Certification marks on products from government agencies, such as ISI or BIS and star labels for electricity use, confirm that a product meets minimum quality standards. Consumers can also check online reviews.
Consumers have rights, such as the right to safety, information and to choose, and responsibilities, such as checking weight, price, date and quality before buying. A product without a logo or certification mark may not meet standards, so check before you buy. A star-labelled appliance can reduce your electricity bill and also help the environment.

problem.en: Onion supply falls sharply during a flood while demand stays the same. What happens to price?

text.en: Supply decreases while demand stays.
Buyers compete for fewer onions.
The price rises.

why.en: Low supply with steady demand raises prices.

problem.en: A packet of gram flour is labelled 1 kg but weighs 900 g. What should a consumer do?

text.en: Notice that the weight is wrong.
Report to the shopkeeper and consumer authorities.
Governments inspect weights to protect buyers.

prompt.en: Explain how price is decided and how markets are kept fair.

requiredIdeas.en: Governments set standards, test products and monitor weights.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking a market is only a place.
Thinking price is fixed by sellers alone.

points.en: A market brings buyers and sellers together.
Price is set by demand and supply.
Markets can be physical or online; wholesalers, retailers and distributors form a chain.
Governments and consumers keep markets fair.
